

To begin this memoir, I would like to invoke a quote from late YouTuber Alex “Technoblade”:

*...one day, we'll look back at where we started and be amazed by how far we've come.*

1. ## **The Foundation**: A computer and a dream

### *My introduction to the Internet*

It would be an understatement to say that I had been really online from a young age.

By five years old, I had already been playing around with computers. By six, I knew how to insert a floppy disk into a computer. By ten, I was modding Minecraft. By twelve, I was tricking my friend with a fake Facebook website to get his password and pull a prank.

Like a typical child who had very early unsupervised computer access, I really liked games. My parents were really rooting for me to become a smart, successful person. They installed this educational game called JumpStart that taught me stuff like addition and multiplication. I think this is one of the reasons that I have a natural way with numbers.

**![][image1]**

I also happened to have unsupervised smartphone access at an early age. Aside from playing the usual games like Jetpack Joyride, Temple Runner, Candy Crush, and Minecraft (which we’ll get to later\!), I also found myself tweaking around every single setting of my phone, spending late nights watching YouTube tutorials on Android hacking. 

Eventually, this deep-seated curiosity about tech led me to a fateful Google search: “How to make a game?”

Here, I would learn my first programming language.

### *Learning to code*

My entry into programming wasn't high-end. It started with Batch scripts. They were clunky, primitive lines of code. Any seasoned programmer wouldn’t seriously use this for a game. However, for a kid like me, the wonder of being able to program a computer sparked immense joy in me. It felt like magic the second that my games actually executed

![][image2]

I got hooked on the feeling of creation. I wanted to make games on a larger scale. I wanted to actually be able to control a player. After searching for more avenues to let out my creative itch, I ended up following a Java tutorial for ten days straight. I was hooked. I was barely coming away from my computer. I knew I had to make this game.

![][image3]

After those grueling hours trying to understand and debug my code, I finally came up with my own game called Tanky. The objective was simple: protect the core. I uploaded this on [itch.io](http://itch.io), a game publishing site, and got a small bit of traction.

![][image4]

Publishing a game was like giving a piece of myself on the Internet. I didn’t know at the time that I would do way more of that.

### *Minecraft*

Minecraft is a sandbox game where you can create whatever you want and do whatever you like. As a kid, this concept immediately appealed to me. I started out on Pocket Edition, hunched over a small smartphone screen, but eventually, I made the jump to playing on my computer. That transition changed everything.

Remember how I learned how to program in Java? The thing is that Minecraft was also programmed in Java. This way, I knew how to make modifications to the game. This game became my avenue to create everything I wanted to. 

In Minecraft, there are these things called *servers*, kind of like virtual rooms people could host to let many players play on the same world at the same time.

![][image5]

At the time, I was playing on a Dutch server called NLGVNL. Even though I didn't speak the language, I was obsessed with how the server worked. I saw the "scaffolding" behind the curtain like the plugins, the permissions, and how the server was administered.

One day, I was asked to contribute to a server’s development. That was the moment the veil lifted. I realized a server wasn't just a map. It was an intricate machine that needed a dutiful architect to take care of it.

This would eventually lead to me making my own server. 

2. ## **The Build**: The making of HearthCraft 

### *The Piso Net*

In 2018, I decided to build my own world: HearthCraft. Our motto? **Home is where the hearth is.**

The timing was terrible. My laptop was broken, so I was stuck coding Java on my phone and walking to the neighborhood "piso net" to push updates. I would sit in those cramped, coin-operated internet booths and debug a global server while the timer ticked down on my coins.

![][image6]

Then there was the money. Servers cost money, and as a teenager in the Philippines, international payments were a nightmare. I had to make my parents sign consent forms just so I could use PayMaya and GCash to keep the hosting alive. I was basically running a global startup before I was old enough to own a credit card. 

At this time, I was still struggling to learn how to code. This time, I wasn’t just making a standalone game. I actually needed to know how computers work. I needed to know how to make a game in which hundreds of people could play at the same time. Aside from that, at the ripe age of 14, I needed to know how to set up payment systems to gather funds for my server. 

Aside from being the developer, I did everything: graphic design, marketing, community management, chat moderation, and other responsibilities. As a teen, I was as free and unemployed as you could get and I was taking advantage of it.

### *The Pandemic & Takeoff*

Eventually, the server got traction. The player count grew over time. Because of the money I obtained from my Minecraft server, I was eventually able to afford myself a 30,000 Php second-hand, high-performing laptop. 

Then the pandemic struck.

People were stuck to their homes. It became even worse when people are stuck in places that they cannot even call home. The world, to many, seemed cold and callous.

I took on the challenge to move from creating a game to building a community. People from all over the world would come to the server\! I had the pleasure to meet many people who come from very diverse perspectives and very different life situations.

![][image7]

As the manager of an online community more than the developer of a unique game, I had the responsibility to support a safe space. This meant that I always had to be present on the server. During online classes, I would always have my server in the background.

Of course, managing an online community isn’t easy. People naturally tend to conflict for some reason or another. While this was, in hindsight, emotional labor, it gave me the insight I needed to keep the server on for almost seven years.

What I loved about Minecraft specifically was that if you get a ton of people in a space where creation is limitless, the result is pretty amazing. People built projects on a massive scale. They took builds very seriously, and used these as a medium to bond with other players.

![][image8]

The server would go on to serve more than **40,000** players. The growth wasn't just a number on a dashboard. It was a shift in my entire reality. Managing HearthCraft during the pandemic made me realize that I was working on real stuff. Suddenly, I wasn't just a hobbyist tweaking a game or installing mods. I was creating digital infrastructure, which was particularly satisfying for my natural tendency to build. My days were a blur of attending lectures and my nights were spent troubleshooting and managing a volunteer staff team that spanned multiple time zones.

This was the "takeoff" point where the server transitioned from a project into a legitimate source of income. It was paying for my tuition and my daily expenses, effectively turning my childhood curiosity into a career before I had even graduated high school.

### *Saying Goodbye*

At some point, the scale of HearthCraft had reached a point where it felt more like a heavy responsibility than a creative outlet. Everything started to feel like a chore, but because the entire ecosystem relied on my presence as the owner, I couldn't simply walk away. I hadn't been able to find a successor to take over the intricate machine I had built, and I realized I couldn't maintain the server while moving forward in my professional career.

![][image9]

On the 6th anniversary of the server, I bought a cake to celebrate, not knowing it would be the last one. When the decision was finally made to shut down, the community gathered to say one last goodbye. It was deeply satisfying to see that I had built something people truly cared about.

![][image10]

In April 2025, I made the final, heartbreaking decision to shut it down. I didn’t see myself doing Minecraft for much longer. I had to break the news to the players and this was really heartbreaking for me. I remember crying really hard because I had to say goodbye to almost seven years of work. We built a massive "GOODBYE\!\!" sign in the world and gathered everyone for one last time.

![][image11]

And as the lights began to dim on the server, the people who had lived there for years began to pour their hearts out on Discord.

The messages were a testament to the fact that I had made something people truly wanted. One player, Hurricane, shared a journey that spanned their entire youth:

"Wow...so much time has passed since I first joined this server... 5 years of memories that I will cherish even more once this server is gone.... everything from getting banned by nearly every mod at the time in 2020, to all of the amazing nights hanging out at the flower casino... from raging at Ducky and Cat in the old pvp arena to selling my 4x pufferfish farm to Laf for $108 million, I have created so many memories with so many of you here since I was in middle school, September 2020, to now being in college here in 2025."

![][image12]

Another player, fishxbones, noted how the server had cracked their shell:

"wellll it's probably the first and the last time i actually got attached to a server like that. i wasn't really the type to chat much or hang out with people in-game, but the whole community was always so chill, helpful and welcoming... also huge thanks for not pulling the plug right away, which gave me enough time to finish my last monstrosity little act of appreciation."

![][image13]

As the final players logged off, I realized how true the server’s motto had become: that home is really where the hearth is. I was left with the profound realization that while the digital world was gone, the memories and the version of myself it helped build were permanent.

3. ## **The Finished Structure**: After HearthCraft

### *Enrolling into Computer Science*

Because of the years I spent in the trenches of server development, enrolling in Computer Science felt less like starting a new path and more like finally learning the formal language for what I had already built. I entered my degree already understanding that code isn't just text on a screen. While other students were learning their first loops, I was applying those concepts to the real-world problems I had faced in the "piso net" years earlier. 

I also went into UP with unique soft skills that you couldn’t just get anywhere. Learning how to organize people and lead a team got me much of the opportunities that I enjoy today. My experience was a perfect balance of learning both technical and leadership skills. 

### *Sharing my Lessons*

As I transitioned into a professional career in software engineering, I realized that I still have a deep passion for teaching. I now get invited to speak at events to give insights into the field, and I always find myself coming back to my Minecraft career. People are often surprised by what a "block game" can teach a professional engineer, but I’m always grateful to share the insights I got to others. 
![][image14]

### *Forward*

![][image15]

In Minecraft, a scaffolding block is a unique utility used for construction. You can stack them from the ground up to reach great heights, but they are designed to be temporary. Once the permanent building is finished, you hit the bottom block, and the entire structure collapses, leaving only the permanent build standing.

HearthCraft was the scaffolding of my life. It was a phase, but also forever part of me. It was a messy structure, as messy as a teenager owning a startup can get, that allowed me to reach heights I couldn't have navigated on my own. When I shut HearthCraft down, I hit that bottom block. The scaffolding has finally been taken down, the "Goodbye" signs have been posted, and the server is offline. 

In the thousands of hours I spent in this game, I was being built from the ground up. While this server was temporary, the technical expertise, the drive to build community, and a sense of entrepreneurship on the side remains rock solid in my heart.
